Differentially Private Non-convex Distributionally Robust Optimization

Difei Xu Affiliation: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology    Meng Ding Affiliation: State University of New York at Buffalo    Zebin Ma Affiliation: Provable Responsible AI and Data Analytics (PRADA) Lab Affiliation: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology    Huanyi Xie Affiliation: Provable Responsible AI and Data Analytics (PRADA) Lab Affiliation: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology    Youming Tao Affiliation: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology Affiliation: Technische Universität Berlin    Aicha Slaitane Affiliation: Provable Responsible AI and Data Analytics (PRADA) Lab Affiliation: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology    Di Wang Affiliation:  Affiliation: Provable Responsible AI and Data Analytics (PRADA) Lab Affiliation: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
Abstract

Real-world deployments routinely face distribution shifts, group imbalances, and adversarial perturbations, under which the traditional Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) framework can degrade severely. Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) addresses this issue by optimizing the worst-case expected loss over an uncertainty set of distributions, offering a principled approach to robustness. Meanwhile, as training data in DRO always involves sensitive information, safeguarding it against leakage under Differential Privacy (DP) is essential. In contrast to classical DP-ERM, DP-DRO has received much less attention due to its minimax optimization structure with uncertainty constraint. To bridge the gap, we provide a comprehensive study of DP-(finite-sum)-DRO with ψ\psi-divergence and non-convex loss. First, we study DRO with general ψ\psi-divergence by reformulating it as a minimization problem, and develop a novel (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP optimization method, called DP Double-Spider, tailored to this structure. Under mild assumptions, we show that it achieves a utility bound of 𝒪⁡(1n+(d​log⁡(1/δ)n​ε)2/3)\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}+(\frac{\sqrt{d\log(1/\delta)}}{n\varepsilon})^{2/3}) in terms of the gradient norm, where nn denotes the data size and dd denotes the model dimension. We further improve the utility rate for specific divergences. In particular, for DP-DRO with KL-divergence, by transforming the problem into a compositional finite-sum optimization problem, we develop a DP Recursive-Spider method and show that it achieves a utility bound of 𝒪⁡((d​log⁡(1/δ)n​ε)2/3)\mathcal{O}((\frac{\sqrt{d\log(1/\delta)}}{n\varepsilon})^{2/3}), matching the best-known result for non-convex DP-ERM. Experimentally, we demonstrate that our proposed methods outperform existing approaches for DP minimax optimization.

1 Introduction

With the rapid expansion of machine learning in real-world applications, the demand for robust model training has become increasingly critical. Conventional Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) aims to minimize the expected loss under the empirical distribution of the training data, with the hope that the resulting model generalizes well to unseen test data. However, in practice, ERM often struggles when the training and test distributions do not align. Such mismatches are pervasive, including domain shifts in transfer and domain adaptation tasks (Blitzer et al., 2006), imbalanced training datasets where fairness for underrepresented groups is essential (Sagawa et al., 2019), and adversarial perturbations that deliberately mislead deployed models (Goodfellow et al., 2014; Fu et al., 2025; Fu and Wang, 2023; Madry et al., 2017). In these settings, models trained purely with ERM typically exhibit severe performance degradation, limiting their reliability in safety-critical or fairness-sensitive applications. To overcome these limitations, Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) has emerged as a powerful alternative (Ben-Tal et al., 2013; Shapiro, 2017; Rahimian and Mehrotra, 2019). By optimizing performance against the worst-case distribution within a specified uncertainty set, DRO provides models with resilience to distribution shifts, fairness violations, and adversarial attacks. This worst-case perspective has made DRO a central tool in building robust learning systems.

Meanwhile, as the training of DRO often involves private data, safeguarding sensitive information has become a critical priority. Differential privacy (DP) (Dwork et al., 2014) now occupies a central position in data analysis, driven by the growing demand for principled protection guaranties. The foundational work Dwork et al. (2006) established the modern framework for DP, and its incorporation into empirical risk minimization (ERM) has progressed substantially. Early research focused primarily on convex optimization, delivering strong privacy guarantees alongside efficient learning, for example, (Bassily et al., 2014; Bassily et al., 2019; Bassily et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2025; Huai et al., 2020; Su et al., 2023; Tao et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2020a; Wang et al., 2020b; Wang et al., 2017). More recently, attention has shifted toward non-convex settings. Notable advances such as (Wang et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2020; Xiao et al., 2023; Arora et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2020a; Xiang et al., 2023; Tao et al., 2025; Wang and Xu, 2020) tighten error bounds for non-convex optimization while balancing privacy and utility in stochastic gradient methods. However, relatively few studies have focused on (finite-sum) DRO, which involves minimax optimization over an uncertainty set.

Recently, several works have begun to investigate DP-DRO Zhou and Bassily (2024); Selvi et al. (2025). However, these studies either consider only a special classes of DRO (such as group DRO Zhou and Bassily (2024)) or propose methods that are not scalable to large datasets (Selvi et al., 2025). DRO with ψ\psi-divergence, a widely used framework in machine learning, has not yet been systematically studied under DP. This gap motivates the present work. Although DRO can be formulated as a minimax problem, it differs fundamentally from classical minimax optimization. As a result, recent advances in DP minimax optimization cannot be directly applied to analyze or solve DP-DRO due to their assumptions on the loss function or the absence of uncertainty sets (see Appendix A for details).

To fill this gap, we provide the first systematic study of DP-(finite-sum) DRO with ψ\psi-divergence and non-convex loss. First, by establishing a primal–dual equivalence for distributionally robust optimization, we reduce the original minimax problem to an unconstrained minimization problem over model parameters and a dual variable. Building on this reformulation, we develop a novel private optimization method called DP Double-Spider, which is a differentially private and non-trivial extension of SPIDER (Fang et al., 2018) from ERM to DRO. DP Double-Spider alternates updates of the primal and dual variables using variance-reduced stochastic gradients perturbed with calibrated Gaussian noises, which outperforms classical DP-SGD-based methods such as DP-SGDA. Theoretically, under mild assumptions, we show that the utility of the resulting private model, measured by the gradient norm, is upper bounded by 𝒪⁡(1n+(d​log⁡(1/δ)n​ε)2/3)\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}+(\frac{\sqrt{d\log(1/\delta)}}{n\varepsilon})^{2/3}), where nn is the data size and dd is the model dimension.

We then consider improving the utility bound of the above method. Specifically, we focus on DRO with KL divergence. Specifically, rather than introducing dual variables, the problem can be rewritten as a compositional minimization problem. Based on this, we develop our follow our idea DP-Double Spider and propose DP Recursive-Spider. Theoretically, we show that the utility rate can be improved to 𝒪⁡((d​log⁡(1/δ)n​ε)2/3)\mathcal{O}\!\left(\bigl(\tfrac{\sqrt{d\log(1/\delta)}}{n\varepsilon}\bigr)^{\!2/3}\right), which matches the best-known result in DP-ERM with non-convex loss Arora et al. (2023). It is notable that this is also the first result on DP compositional optimization.

Our contribution can be summarized as below:

  1. 1.

    A generic DP-DRO framework: For DRO with general ψ\psi-divergence, based on its one primal-dual equivalent formulation, we propose the Differentially Private Double SPIDER algorithm to deal with both the primal and dual variables simultaneously. We claim that the algorithm is (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP and the utility of our private model is 𝒪⁡(1n+(d​log⁡(1/δ)n​ε)2/3)\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}+(\frac{\sqrt{d\log(1/\delta)}}{n\varepsilon})^{2/3}).

  2. 2.

    A DP method for DRO with KL-divergence: For DRO with KL-divergence, we further improve its utility. Specifically, we propose DP Recursive-Spider and show its private model achieves an utility bound of 𝒪⁡((d​log⁡(1/δ)n​ε)2/3)\mathcal{O}((\frac{\sqrt{d\log(1/\delta)}}{n\varepsilon})^{2/3}).

  3. 3.

    We implement our algorithms on the constructed imbalanced dataset CIFAR10-ST, MINST-ST and the inherently imbalanced dataset CelebA and Fashion-MNIST. Our results demonstrate that our algorithms perform better than the previous baselines across distinct datasets and privacy budgets, providing empirical support for our theoretical analysis.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Differential Privacy

Definition 1 (Differential Privacy (Dwork et al., 2006)).

Given a data universe 𝒳\mathcal{X}, we say that two datasets S,S′⊆𝒳S,S^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{X} are neighbors if they differ by only one entry, which is denoted as S∼S′S\sim S^{\prime}. A randomized algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} is (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-differentially private (DP) if for all neighboring datasets S,S′S,S^{\prime} and for all events EE in the output space of 𝒜\mathcal{A}, the following holds

ℙ⁡(𝒜⁡(S)∈E)⩽eε​ℙ​(𝒜⁡(S′)∈E)+δ.\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{A}(S)\in E)\leqslant e^{\varepsilon}\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{A}(S^{\prime})\in E)+\delta.

If δ=0\delta=0, we call algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} ε\varepsilon-DP.

Definition 2.

Given a function q:𝒵→ℝdq:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}, we say qq has Δ2​(q)\Delta_{2}(q) ℓ2\ell_{2}-sensitivity if for any neighboring datasets D,D′D,D^{\prime} we have ‖q⁡(D)−q⁡(D′)‖⩽Δ2​(q)\|q(D)-q(D^{\prime})\|\leqslant\Delta_{2}(q).

Definition 3.

Given any function q:𝒵→ℝdq:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}, the Gaussian mechanism is defined as q⁡(D)+ξq(D)+\xi where ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,Δ22​(q)​log⁡(1.25/δ)ε2​𝐈d)\xi\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\frac{\Delta_{2}^{2}(q)\log(1.25/\delta)}{\varepsilon^{2}}\mathbf{I}_{d}\right). Gaussian mechanism preserves (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP for 0<ε,δ≤10<\varepsilon,\delta\leq 1.

2.2 Distributionally Robust Optimization

As we mentioned earlier, unlike Empirical Risk Minimization, there are different formulations of DRO for various applications. In this paper, we will focus on the fine-sum version of DRO with an uncertainty set, which is the most commonly used model in deep learning to handle distribution shift (Levy et al., 2020; Jin et al., 2021; Qi et al., 2021; Sinha et al., 2017). Given an underlying data distribution P0P_{0} and a loss ℓ\ell, DRO aims to find a model x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} that minimizes the loss over all data that is close to the distribution P0P_{0}:

minx∈ℝd⁡maxP∈𝒰⁡(P0)​𝔼ξ∼P​[ℓ⁡(x,ξ)],\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\max_{P\in\mathcal{U}(P_{0})}\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim P}[\ell(x;\xi)],

where 𝒰⁡(P0)\mathcal{U}(P_{0}) is an uncertainty set for P0P_{0}. Specifically, when 𝒰⁡(P0)={P:Dψ​(P,P0)≤ρ}\mathcal{U}(P_{0})=\{P:D_{\psi}(P,P_{0})\leq\rho\} for some divergence DψD_{\psi} and radius ρ\rho, we refer to the problem as DRO with divergence DψD_{\psi}. It includes the χ2\chi^{2}-divergence, KL-divergence, and the Cressie–Read family, defined as

Dψ(Q∥P0)=∑x∈𝒳p0(x)ψ(q⁡(x)p0​(x)),D_{\psi}(Q\|P_{0})=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}p_{0}(x)\psi\left(\frac{q(x)}{p_{0}(x)}\right), (1)

where ψ\psi is a non-negative convex function satisfying ψ⁡(1)=0\psi(1)=0 and ψ⁡(t)=+∞\psi(t)=+\infty for all t<0t<0.

In this paper, we consider the empirical form of DRO. Specifically, given a training data S={ξi}i=1nS=\{\xi_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}, an equivalent form of DRO with ψ\psi-divergence can be formulated as the following constrained minimax optimization problem:

minx∈ℝd⁡ℱ⁡(x):=max⁡∑i=1np∈Δn⁡pi​ℓ​(x,ξi)−λ0​Dψ​(p,1n​𝕀),\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathcal{F}(x):=\max_{p\in\Delta_{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}\ell(x;\xi_{i})-\lambda_{0}D_{\psi}(p,\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{I}), (2)

where 1n​𝕀\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{I} is the empirical distribution and Δn={𝐩∈ℝn:∑i=1npi=1,pi⩾0}\Delta_{n}=\{\mathbf{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i}=1,p_{i}\geqslant 0\} denotes a nn-dimensional simplex. The hyperparameter λ0\lambda_{0} is pre-specified and remains fixed during training.

Definition 4 (DP-DRO).

In the problem of DP-DRO, given a training data SS, we aim to develop an (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} for solving problem (2). Moreover, we need to make the utility of the private model 𝔼⁡[‖ℱ⁡(𝒜⁡(S))‖]\mathbb{E}[\|\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{A}(S))\|] to be as small as possible, where the expectation takes over the randomness of the algorithm.

In the following, we will impose several assumptions on the problem for our theoretical utility analysis.

Definition 5.

A function f:ℝd→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} is GG-Lipschitz continuous if ∀x,y∈ℝd\forall x,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, |f⁡(w1,x)−f⁡(w2,x)|⩽G⁡‖w1−w2‖\left|f(w_{1};x)-f(w_{2};x)\right|\leqslant G\left\|w_{1}-w_{2}\right\|, where G>0G>0 is some finite constant.

Definition 6.

A differentiable function f:ℝd→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} is LL-smooth if ∀x,y∈ℝd\forall x,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, we have ‖∇f​(x)−∇f​(y)‖⩽L⁡‖x−y‖\left\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\right\|\leqslant L\left\|x-y\right\|, where L>0L>0 is some finite constant.

It is noteworthy that Lipschitz and LL-smoothness are commonly adopted in optimization research (Zhang et al., 2025b; Qi et al., 2021; Qi et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2025c; Xue et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2022). However, as we will mention later, DRO with ψ\psi-divergence may not satisfy smoothness but a more general property called generalized smoothness.

Definition 7 (Generalized (L0,L1)(L_{0},L_{1})-smooth).

A differentiable function f:ℝd→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} is genenralized (L0,L1)(L_{0},L_{1})-smooth if for any x,y∈ℝdx,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, we have that ‖∇xf​(x)−∇xf​(y)‖⩽(L0+L1​‖∇xf​(x)‖)​‖x−y‖\left\|\nabla_{x}f(x)-\nabla_{x}f(y)\right\|\leqslant(L_{0}+L_{1}\left\|\nabla_{x}f(x)\right\|)\left\|x-y\right\|, where L0,L1>0L_{0},L_{1}>0 are some finite constants.

Definition 8.

A function ψ∗\psi^{*} called the conjugate function, given ψ\psi, is defined as ψ∗​(t)=supa∈ℝ{t​a−ψ⁡(a)}\psi^{*}(t)=\sup_{a\in\mathbb{R}}\{ta-\psi(a)\}.

Assumptions. Generally, we focus on the non-convex and smooth loss function ℓ\ell.

Assumption 1.

For any sample ξ∈𝒟\xi\in\mathcal{D}, the loss function ℓ⁡(x,ξ)\ell(x,\xi) is GG-Lipschitz continuous and LL-smooth in xx.

The smoothness of the primal function alone is insufficient for guarantee the smoothness of its conjugate. To support our analysis, we therefore impose the following additional assumption, which is commonly applied for a wide range of ψ\psi-divergence, where instances can be found in Table 1.

Assumption 2.

The conjugate function ψ∗\psi^{*} of ψ\psi is MM-smooth.

Assumption 3.

Assume that the domain of the conjugate function ψ∗\psi^{*} is bounded by a constant S0>0S_{0}>0. Also, ψ∗\psi^{*} remains non-negative on its domain.

3 DP Double-SPIDER

In this section, we will consider the general ψ\psi-divergence. Due to the divergence regularization and the constrained simplex, it is hard to optimize efficiently. Thus, a popular approach is to investigate its dual formulation. By strong duality (Levy et al., 2020; Shapiro, 2017), we can reformulate the objective function (2) as

minx⁡Ψ⁡(x)=infη∈ℝℒ^​(x,η):=λn​∑i=1nψ∗​(ℓ⁡(x,ξi)−ηλ)+η,\min_{x}\Psi(x)=\inf_{\eta\in\mathbb{R}}\hat{\mathcal{L}}(x,\eta):=\frac{\lambda}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi^{*}(\frac{\ell(x;\xi_{i})-\eta}{\lambda})+\eta, (3)

where η∈ℝ\eta\in\mathbb{R} is a dual variable. To simplify the discussion below, we define ℒ​(x,η)=ℒ^​(x,G​η)\mathcal{L}(x,\eta)=\hat{\mathcal{L}}(x,G\eta). Note that there are different forms of the dual problem; each will lead to different methods. The form of duality adopted in this work differs from the classical dual-based approach (Rafique et al., 2022).

Under Assumptions 1 and 2, the function Ψ⁡(x)\Psi(x) is differentiable. With this reformulation, Jin et al. (2021) showed that ‖∇x,ηℒ​(x,η)‖⩽α/2\|\nabla_{x,\eta}\mathcal{L}(x,\eta)\|\leqslant\alpha/\sqrt{2} directly implies ‖∇ℱ​(x)‖⩽α\|\nabla\mathcal{F}(x)\|\leqslant\alpha. Thus, our goal is to find private x,ηx,\eta to make ‖∇x,ηℒ​(x,η)‖\|\nabla_{x,\eta}\mathcal{L}(x,\eta)\| as small as possible.

Note that problem (3) is a finite-sum minimization problem. Specifically, let z=(x,η)z=(x,\eta) and ℒ⁡(x,η,𝒮):=1|𝒮|​∑i=1|𝒮|ℒ⁡(x,η,ξi)\mathcal{L}(x,\eta;\mathcal{S}):=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|}\sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{S}|}\mathcal{L}(x,\eta;\xi_{i}) with ℒ⁡(x,η,ξi)=λ​ψ∗​(ℓ⁡(x,ξi)−ηλ)+η\mathcal{L}(x,\eta;\xi_{i})=\lambda\psi^{*}(\frac{\ell(x;\xi_{i})-\eta}{\lambda})+\eta. Thus, one direct way is directly adopting the previous method for DP-ERM, such as DP-SGD (Bassily et al., 2014; Abadi et al., 2016b; Wang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a) on the single composite variable z=(x,η)z=(x,\eta). In particular, we may use DP-SPIDER (Arora et al., 2023), which achieves the best-known rate for DP-ERM with non-convex loss.

However, due to the specific structure of Ψ\Psi in (3), directly using these methods may lead to sub-optimal performance. The main reason is that, under Assumptions 1 and 2, (Zhang et al., 2025b) showed that ℒ⁡(x,η,ξi)\mathcal{L}(x,\eta;\xi_{i}) is (L0,L1)(L_{0},L_{1})-smooth in xx but L2L_{2}-smooth in η\eta, with L0=G+G2​MλL_{0}=G+\frac{G^{2}M}{\lambda}, L1=L/GL_{1}=L/G and L2=G2​MλL_{2}=\frac{G^{2}M}{\lambda}. Due to different smooth properties, training xx and η\eta uniformly will lead to worse noise added in each iteration. In particular, for a fixed xx, the function ℒ⁡(x,⋅)\mathcal{L}(x,\cdot) is smooth, which facilitates a more accurate estimation of the gradient ∇ηℒ\nabla_{\eta}\mathcal{L}. Treating zz as a single variable, however, fails to exploit this property. By instead handling the parameter xx and the dual variable η\eta separately, we can more precisely characterize and control the behavior of the gradient estimators.

Motivated by this, we proposed our DP Double-SPIDER(see Algorithm 2 for details), a private extension of SPIDER for DRO (Zhang et al., 2025b), which is a variance-reduction optimization method based on SPIDER Fang et al. (2018) that achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) convergence in the non-private case. Specifically, each variable is updated using a SPIDER-style variance-reduced gradient estimator perturbed with Gaussian noise. Concretely, in Line 4, for η\eta, we perform a large-batch refresh every qq iterations with batch size N1N_{1} to form a low-variance estimate, and in Line 6 for the remaining q−1q-1 steps, we use incremental corrections with mini-batch size N2N_{2} via gradient differences, adding an independent Gaussian noise term at each step for privacy. After updating η\eta, we repeat the same refresh–increment pattern for xx, using batch sizes N3N_{3} and N4N_{4}, again injecting calibrated Gaussian noise. This alternating procedure—refresh once, then correct q−1q-1 times—controls stochastic variance while enforcing privacy, yielding coordinated updates of η\eta and xx every qq iterations.

Note that there are two differences compared with the non-private one: (1) As we mentioned, due to the different smooth properties of xx and η\eta, we need the variance-reduced gradient estimator for ∇ηℒ\nabla_{\eta}\mathcal{L} and ∇xℒ\nabla_{x}\mathcal{L} individually, i.e., it is a double version of SPIDER. (2) Under Assumptions 1 and 2, we can show that the sensitivity of the gradient difference in the variance-reduced gradient estimator, such as ∇xℒ​(xt,ηt+1,ℬ)−∇xℒ​(xt−1,ηt,ℬ)\nabla_{x}\mathcal{L}(x_{t},\eta_{t+1};\mathcal{B})-\nabla_{x}\mathcal{L}(x_{t-1},\eta_{t};\mathcal{B}), is O⁡(max⁡{‖xt−xt−1‖,‖ηt+1−ηt‖})O(\max\{\|x_{t}-x_{t-1}\|,\|\eta_{t+1}-\eta_{t}\|\}). Thus, the Gaussian noise added to ensure DP also depends on such differences, making the analysis complicated.

The following (draft) results provide privacy and utility guarantees of DP Double-SPIDER. For the full versions and their proofs, we refer readers to Appendix.

Theorem 1.

For any ε>0\varepsilon>0 and δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), let σ1=𝒪⁡(C1​T​log⁡(1/δ)n​q​ε)\sigma_{1}=\mathcal{O}(\frac{C_{1}\sqrt{T\log(1/\delta)}}{n\sqrt{q}\varepsilon}), σ2=𝒪⁡(C2​log⁡(1/δ)N2​ε)\sigma_{2}=\mathcal{O}(\frac{C_{2}\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}}{N_{2}\varepsilon}). Similarly, set σ3=𝒪⁡(C3​T​log⁡(1/δ)n​q​ε)\sigma_{3}=\mathcal{O}(\frac{C_{3}\sqrt{T\log(1/\delta)}}{n\sqrt{q}\varepsilon}) and σ4=𝒪⁡(C4​log⁡(1/δ)ε​max⁡{1N4,Tn​q})\sigma_{4}=\mathcal{O}(\frac{C_{4}\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}}{\varepsilon}\max\{\frac{1}{N_{4}},\frac{\sqrt{T}}{n\sqrt{q}}\}), Algorithm 2 is (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP.

Theorem 2.

Under Assumption 1-3, with the parameter settings in Theorem 1 and some specific values of {Ni}i=14\{N_{i}\}_{i=1}^{4}, {Ci}i=14\{C_{i}\}_{i=1}^{4}, TT, qq and step size α,β\alpha,\beta in Algorithm 2, we have the following guarantee:

𝔼​‖∇ℱ​(x)‖⩽𝒪⁡(1n+(d​log⁡(1/δ)n​ε)23).\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\mathcal{F}(x)\|\leqslant\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}+(\frac{\sqrt{d\log(1/\delta)}}{n\varepsilon})^{\frac{2}{3}}). (4)
Remark 1.

For DP-ERM with model size dd and data size nn, it has been shown that the utility bound given by DP-SGD is O⁡((d​log⁡(1/δ)n​ε)12)O\big((\frac{\sqrt{d\log(1/\delta)}}{n\varepsilon})^{\frac{1}{2}}\big) (Wang and Xu, 2019). Thus, by adopting the proof in (Zhang et al., 2025b), we can show the same bound when using DP-SGD to (3). Comparing the bound of O⁡(max⁡{1n,(d​log⁡(1/δ)n​ε)2/3})O(\max\{\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}},(\frac{\sqrt{d\log(1/\delta)}}{n\varepsilon})^{2/3}\}) in Theorem 1, we can see that Algorithm 2 is better. The main reason is that, in DP-SGD, the noise we add depends on the l2l_{2}-norm sensitivity of the loss gradient, which is upper bounded by the Lipschitz constant. Thus, by using the composition theorem, adding the same scale of noise to the gradient in each iteration can guarantee DP.

In comparison, in Algorithm 2, we only add noise to the gradient every qq iterations, i.e., T/qT/q times in total, which is significantly smaller than that in DP-SGD. Moreover, when we add noise to the variance-reduced gradient estimator, such as ∇xℒ​(xt,ηt+1,ℬ)−∇xℒ​(xt−1,ηt,ℬ)\nabla_{x}\mathcal{L}(x_{t},\eta_{t+1};\mathcal{B})-\nabla_{x}\mathcal{L}(x_{t-1},\eta_{t};\mathcal{B}), its sensitivity is O⁡(max⁡{‖xt−xt−1‖,‖ηt+1−ηt‖})O(\max\{\|x_{t}-x_{t-1}\|,\|\eta_{t+1}-\eta_{t}\|\}). Thus, when tt becomes larger, we can show the noise we add becomes smaller than that in DP-SGD.

Remark 2.

Note that there is a term 1n\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} in the utility bound. This term comes from the estimation process of using the large batch size N1,N3N_{1},N_{3}, where we take all samples to estimate the gradient as the anchor point in preparation for the next q−1q-1 updates. After that, accumulating the other q−1q-1 gradient variations with the parameter setting we present in the theorem leads to the term with privacy parameters.

4 Improved Rates via DP Recursive-SPIDER

Recall that for DP-ERM with non-convex loss, the best-known result for utility is 𝒪⁡((dn​ε)2/3)\mathcal{O}((\frac{\sqrt{d}}{n\varepsilon})^{2/3}) (Arora et al., 2023). Thus, from Theorem 1, we can see that Algorithm 2 achieves the same result only if n≤O⁡(d2)n\leq O(d^{2}). Thus, a natural question is whether we can further improve the bound for DP-DRO? In this section, we will provide an affirmative answer for DRO with KL-divergence.

For DP-DRO with KL-divergence, besides the dual problem in (3), it has been shown that the problem can be reformulated as the following compositional finite-sum optimization problem (Qi et al., 2022) with some ρ\rho, which will be the main focus of this section:

minx⁡minλ≥λ0⁡Ψ⁡(x,λ):=λ​log⁡(1n​∑i=1nexp⁡(ℓ⁡(x,ξi)λ))+λ​ρ.\min_{x}\min_{\lambda\geq\lambda_{0}}\Psi(x,\lambda):=\lambda\log(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\exp(\frac{\ell(x;\xi_{i})}{\lambda}))+\lambda\rho. (5)

Specifically, by considering 𝐰=(xT,λ)T∈ℝd+1\mathbf{w}=(x^{T},\lambda)^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1} as a single variable to be optimized, the objective function is a compositional function of 𝐰\mathbf{w} in the form of f⁡(g⁡(𝐰))f(g(\mathbf{w})), where g⁡(𝐰)=[g1,g2]=[λ,1n​∑i=1nexp⁡(ℓ⁡(x,ξi)λ)]∈ℝ2g(\mathbf{w})=[g_{1},g_{2}]=\left[\lambda,\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\exp\left(\frac{\ell(x;\xi_{i})}{\lambda}\right)\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{2} and f⁡(g)=g1​log⁡(g2)+g1​ρf(g)=g_{1}\log(g_{2})+g_{1}\rho. For convenience, we define g⁡(𝐰,ξ)=exp⁡(ℓ⁡(x,ξ)λ)g(\mathbf{w};\xi)=\exp(\frac{\ell(x;\xi)}{\lambda}). The gradient of Ψ⁡(𝐰)\Psi(\mathbf{w}) is given by:

∇xΨ​(𝐰)=∇f​(g⁡(𝐰))​∇xg​(𝐰)\displaystyle\nabla_{x}\Psi(\mathbf{w})=\nabla f(g(\mathbf{w}))\nabla_{x}g(\mathbf{w})
∇λΨ​(𝐰)=∇f​(g⁡(𝐰))​∇λg​(𝐰)+log⁡(g⁡(𝐰))+ρ.\displaystyle\nabla_{\lambda}\Psi(\mathbf{w})=\nabla f(g(\mathbf{w}))\nabla_{\lambda}g(\mathbf{w})+\log(g(\mathbf{w}))+\rho.

Note that since ff is independent of the data. Thus, it is sufficient to develop a private estimator for g⁡(𝐰)g(\mathbf{w}), ∇xg​(𝐰)\nabla_{x}g(\mathbf{w}), and ∇λg​(𝐰)\nabla_{\lambda}g(\mathbf{w}). Similar to problem (3), we can see that xx and λ\lambda play different roles. Thus, when considering DP, we need to treat them separately, which motivates our DP Recursive-Spider (see Algorithm 3 for details). DP Recursive-Spider adopts a similar idea as in DP Double-Spider, where we use a private variance-reduced gradient estimator for both ∇xg​(𝐰)\nabla_{x}g(\mathbf{w}) and ∇λg​(𝐰)\nabla_{\lambda}g(\mathbf{w}) in each iteration. The algorithm proceeds in phases of length qq, during which it alternately updates xx and η\eta in each iteration. At the beginning of each phase (Lines 7–8), the gradient estimators are computed via empirical mean and subsequently privatized with Gaussian noise. In Lines 13–14, the estimators 𝐮t\mathbf{u}_{t} and vtv_{t} are updated via gradient variation for the subsequent q−1q-1 iterations. After obtaining the gradient estimate of g⁡(𝐰)g(\mathbf{w}), the function value g⁡(𝐰)g(\mathbf{w}) is recursively estimated in Line 16. This is motivated by STORM (Cutkosky and Orabona, 2019), which could provide a better estimate of g⁡(𝐰)g(\mathbf{w}). It is noteworthy that as βt→0\beta_{t}\to 0, sts_{t} approaches the gradient variation, whereas when βt→1\beta_{t}\to 1, sts_{t} behaves like the empirical mean.

The following (draft) results provide privacy and utility guarantees of DP Recursive-Spider. For the full versions and their proofs, we refer readers to Appendix.

Theorem 3.

For any ε>0\varepsilon>0 and δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), let σ1=σ3=𝒪⁡(T​log⁡(1/δ)n​q​ε)\sigma_{1}=\sigma_{3}=\mathcal{O}(\frac{\sqrt{T\log(1/\delta)}}{nq\varepsilon}), σ2=𝒪⁡(‖xt−xt−1‖​log⁡(1/δ)ε​max⁡{1b2,Tn})\sigma_{2}=\mathcal{O}(\|x_{t}-x_{t-1}\|\frac{\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}}{\varepsilon}\max\left\{\frac{1}{b_{2}},\frac{\sqrt{T}}{n}\right\}), σ^2=𝒪⁡(log⁡(1/δ)ε​max⁡{1b2,Tn})\hat{\sigma}_{2}=\mathcal{O}(\frac{\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}}{\varepsilon}\max\left\{\frac{1}{b_{2}},\frac{\sqrt{T}}{n}\right\}). Similarly, we set σ4=𝒪⁡(‖λt−λt−1‖​log⁡(1/δ)ε​max⁡{1b2,Tn})\sigma_{4}=\mathcal{O}(\|\lambda_{t}-\lambda_{t-1}\|\frac{\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}}{\varepsilon}\max\left\{\frac{1}{b_{2}},\frac{\sqrt{T}}{n}\right\}), σ^4=𝒪⁡(log⁡(1/δ)ε​max⁡{1b4,Tn})\hat{\sigma}_{4}=\mathcal{O}(\frac{\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}}{\varepsilon}\max\left\{\frac{1}{b_{4}},\frac{\sqrt{T}}{n}\right\}), and σst=𝒪⁡(T​log⁡(1/δ)n​ε)\sigma_{s_{t}}=\mathcal{O}(\frac{\sqrt{T\log(1/\delta)}}{n\varepsilon}). Then Algorithm 3 is (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP.

Theorem 4.

Under Assumption 1-3, with the parameters settings in Theorem 3 and some specific values of {bi}i=14\{b_{i}\}_{i=1}^{4}, {Ci}i=15\{C_{i}\}_{i=1}^{5}, TT, qq and step size η\eta in Algorithm  3, we can have the following guarantee:

𝔼​[‖∇ℱ​(x)‖]=\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\|\nabla\mathcal{F}(x)\|]= 𝒪⁡((d​log⁡(1/δ)n​ε)2/3).\displaystyle\mathcal{O}\left(\left(\frac{\sqrt{d\log(1/\delta)}}{n\varepsilon}\right)^{2/3}\right).

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setup

Dataset We consider 4 datasets that are widely used for studies in DRO: CIFAR10-ST (Qi et al., 2022), MNIST-ST (Zhang et al., 2025c), CelebA (Sagawa et al., 2019) and Fashion-MNIST. For constructing CIFAR10-ST, we artificially create imbalanced training data, where we only keep the last 100 images of each class for the first half of the classes, while keeping other classes and the test data unchanged. For constructing MNIST-ST, we convert MNIST into a binary task by mapping digits 0-4 →\to to class 0 and 5-9 →\to to class 1, and artificially create imbalanced training data by subsampling the positive class to a target imratio ∈(0,0.5]\in(0,0.5] (fraction of positives); the test split is kept balanced (imratio = 0.5), and training batches are sampled with the same ratio to match the desired imbalance.

Baselines For the comparison of test accuracy, we compare different algorithms for optimizing the minimax problem (2), including DP-SGDA (Rafique et al., 2022) and Private Diff (Zhang et al., 2025c), across different privacy budgets ε\varepsilon on the three above-mentioned datasets. Besides, we take SCDRO (Zhang et al., 2023) as the non-private baseline, which is state-of-the-art.

Evaluation Metrics The evaluation of the selected four algorithms utilizes four primary metrics to assess utility, privacy, and optimization stability. The gradient norm serves as the central metric for measuring utility in terms of convergence to first-order stationary points. Predictive performance is evaluated via test accuracy across varying privacy budgets. To provide a more nuanced view of classifier performance, the Area Under the Curve (ROC AUC) and the F1 score are employed, with the latter specifically highlighting the balance between precision and recall in imbalanced scenarios. Finally, the Membership Inference Attack (MIA) AUC is used as an empirical measure of privacy robustness, where lower values signify superior protection against training data leakage.

Parameter Setup We will use ResNet20 for our model. To make a fair comparison, we will consider DRO with KL-divergence. The constrained parameter ρ\rho is set to be 0.50.5 and λ0\lambda_{0} is set to 1​e−31e-3.. For all experiments, the batch size is 128. In addition, we set privacy budget ε={0.5,1,5,10}\varepsilon=\{0.5,1,5,10\} with δ=1n1.1\delta=\frac{1}{n^{1.1}}.

MIA Experiments

We evaluate the privacy robustness of different differentially private optimization algorithms using membership inference attacks (MIA) on CIFAR10-ST. Experiments are conducted under privacy budgets ε∈{0.1,1,3,5,8,10}\varepsilon\in\{0.1,1,3,5,8,10\}, covering both high-privacy and low-privacy regimes. For each algorithm–privacy budget configuration, we perform five independent runs with different random seeds and report results as mean ±\pm standard deviation. We focus on two DP DRO methods: DP Double SPIDER and DP Recursive SPIDER. Privacy leakage is evaluated using a standard black-box MIA, where the attacker infers whether a data point was part of the training set based solely on the model’s output confidence. Attack performance is measured by the area under the ROC curve (AUC).

5.2 Experimental Results

We conduct experiments on all four datasets and present representative results for three of them here. Additional experimental results are provided in the Appendix.

Test Accuracy Analysis

Table 3 illustrates that our proposed algorithms, DP Double-SPIDER (DP DS) and DP Recursive-SPIDER (RS DRO), consistently outperform the baseline methods (DP-SGDA and PrivateDiff) across nearly all datasets and privacy budget settings. The only exception is the MNIST-ST dataset, where all four algorithms achieve high accuracy (≈99%\approx 99\%), reaching a performance plateau that makes them effectively indistinguishable.

Due to the absence of a pre-trained base model, the absolute accuracy on CIFAR10-ST is lower than on other benchmarks. However, the performance gap between our methods and the baselines is most pronounced on this dataset, particularly under stringent privacy constraints (e.g., ε=0.5\varepsilon=0.5).

We draw several key observations from these results:

  • •

    Performance Across Datasets: On CIFAR10-ST, CelebA, and Fashion-MNIST, our proposed algorithms maintain a clear and significant lead over the baselines. This suggests that our variance-reduction approach is more effective for complex data distributions where gradient noise typically hinders convergence.

  • •

    Impact of Privacy Budget ε\varepsilon: As expected, the test accuracy for all algorithms improves as the privacy budget ε\varepsilon increases. Notably, our algorithms exhibit superior stability; they provide high utility even with very small ε\varepsilon, whereas the baseline methods suffer significantly more from the increased noise required for higher privacy levels.

  • •

    Sensitivity Comparison: The relative improvement in accuracy as ε\varepsilon increases from 0.5 to 10 is more substantial for DP-SGDA and PrivateDiff, especially on CIFAR10-ST. This high sensitivity indicates that these baseline methods are less robust to the noise injection process, while our methods achieve near-optimal utility even with limited privacy budgets.

Gradient Norm Analysis.

Figure 1 illustrates the evolution of gradient norms on CIFAR10-ST, CelebA, Fashion-MNIST, and MNIST-ST, comparing DP-SGD and SGDA with the proposed DP Double SPIDER and DP Recursive SPIDER methods. Across most datasets, the baseline methods exhibit relatively large gradient norms and noticeable oscillations throughout the training process. In particular, DP-SGDA often shows slow convergence with persistent variance, while SGDA displays pronounced fluctuations, especially in later iterations. These behaviors indicate that privacy-induced noise and stochastic saddle-point dynamics hinder stable convergence to stationary points.

In contrast, DP Double SPIDER consistently achieves faster decay and substantially lower variance in gradient norms, reflecting the effectiveness of variance reduction via gradient-difference estimators. DP Recursive SPIDER further enhances stability, maintaining uniformly small gradient norms with minimal oscillations, particularly in the later stages where baseline methods plateau or become unstable. Overall, these results demonstrate that DP Double SPIDER and DP Recursive SPIDER provide significantly more reliable and stable optimization dynamics under differential privacy, leading to improved convergence toward first-order stationary solutions in private nonconvex–strongly-concave optimization.

MIA Experiments

The results of the Membership Inference Attack (MIA) are summarized in Table 2. The empirical data demonstrates that DP Recursive SPIDER consistently outperforms DP Double SPIDER, achieving significantly lower AUC values across all evaluated privacy budgets ε\varepsilon. While DP Double SPIDER exhibits high and nearly static privacy leakage (AUC ≈0.97\approx 0.97) regardless of the privacy budget, DP Recursive SPIDER provides substantially better protection, with AUC values ranging between 0.780.78 and 0.820.82. Furthermore, DP Recursive SPIDER shows greater sensitivity to variations in ε\varepsilon, whereas DP Double SPIDER remains largely unaffected by changes in the privacy budget within the tested range. Overall, the superior privacy-preserving performance of DP Recursive SPIDER is evident across all settings, which aligns with our theoretical analysis.

6 Conclusion

We investigate the Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) problem with differential privacy guarantees for Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) with non-convex loss functions. Specifically, we first analyze the Double SPIDER DRO algorithm, where the objective function is reformulated as a minimization problem via primal-dual transformation. Subsequently, under the same setting, we recast the original objective as a compositional problem; here, the inner component is a finite-sum loss function, a structure that facilitates the application of efficient optimization techniques. Leveraging this, we introduce a Recursive Double SPIDER algorithm inspired by STORM, which achieves improved error bounds. Finally, we evaluate our methods against baselines on four datasets, whose empirical results demonstrate superior performance and corroborate our theoretical analysis.

Appendix A Related Work

DRO Depending on how the uncertain variables are controlled, DRO formulations can be categorized as either constrained, imposing explicit limits on the uncertain variables or regularized, penalizing them through a regularization term in the objective [Levy et al., 2020]. Duchi and Namkoong [2019] further showed that a DRO problem with quadratic regularization in constraint form is equivalent to minimizing the empirical loss augmented by a variance regularization term on itself.

Many primal–dual methods for min–max optimization [Duchi and Namkoong, 2021; Levy et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021; Duchi et al., 2021] assume convexity of the loss function, which restricts their applicability to the broader class of non-convex machine learning problems. For non-convex DRO, existing works [Qi et al., 2021; Qi et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024] typically impose boundedness or even stronger assumptions on the loss ℓ\ell, further limiting their practical relevance.

The connection between compositional functions and DRO formulations has been recognized and exploited in prior work. Dentcheva et al. [2017] investigated the statistical estimation of compositional functionals with applications to conditional-value-at-risk (CVaR) measures, which are closely related to CVaR-constrained DRO, though without considering stochastic optimization algorithms. To the best of our knowledge, Qi et al. [2021] first applied stochastic compositional optimization to KL-regularized DRO problems, while Qi et al. [2022] extended this framework to the more challenging KL-constrained setting.

DP-DRO As we mentioned, currently there is no work on DP for finite-sum DRO with general ψ\psi-divergence, which has been widely adopted in the deep learning community. Recent work on DP-DRO only considered a specific class. In detail, Selvi et al. [] develops a class of mechanisms that enjoy non-asymptotic and unconditional optimality guarantees. [Zhou and Bassily, 2024] investigates worst-group risk minimization (i.e., group DRO) under differential privacy, proposing algorithms that minimize the maximum risk across multiple sub-populations while preserving privacy. It attempts to privatize the given non-private algorithm for convex loss functions. They reach near-optimal guarantees, introducing simple private algorithms. However, in practice, their methods cannot be applied to our continuous uncertainty set.

DP Minimax Optimization As DRO can be regarded as a constrained minimax problem. Therefore, our work is related to the recent methods for DP minimax optimization Yang et al. [2022]; Zhang et al. [2025c]; Zhang et al. [2022]; Zhao et al. [2023]. For example, Yang et al. [2022] analyzes DP-SGDA for stochastic minimax learning using an algorithmic-stability framework. They reach the near-optimal bound for convex-concave objectives using SGDA. Zhang et al. [2025c] study differentially private stochastic minimax optimization in the nonconvex-strongly-concave (NC-SC) regime and give the first general results beyond convex/PL settings. However, without tailored algorithmic design, standard minimax optimization methods cannot be directly applied to DRO problems, rendering the two frameworks fundamentally incomparable. Under the DRO constraint, plain Stochastic Gradient Descent–Ascent (SGDA) fails in the non-convex setting, as it cannot guarantee convergence to an optimal point without the convex–concave structure [Hsieh et al., 2021] or additional structural assumptions on the optimization variables.

However, there are two limitations that make these work unsuitable for our DRO problem. First, previous work only considers either convex-(strongly) concave or non-convex-strongly-concave case, while for DRO with ψ\psi-divergence, it is a non-convex-concave problem. Thus, previous methods cannot be used for analyzing our problem. Second, directly using previous methods to our problem requires performing the project onto the simplex in each update, which is prohibitively costly. In our work, we address these limitations and we further improve the utility bound for DRO compared to previous methods.

where we define LΨL_{\Psi}, LgL_{g} as the Lipschitz constant of function F⁡(𝐰)F(\mathbf{w}) and g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot) respectively. This completes the proof. ∎

Lemma 8.

where the inequality (a) uses the inequality (x+y)1/3−x1/3≤yx−2/33(x+y)^{1/3}-x^{1/3}\leq\frac{yx^{-2/3}}{3}, the inequality (b) is due to m≥2​σ2m\geq 2\sigma^{2}, and the inequality (c) is due to ηt≤14​LΨ\eta_{t}\leq\frac{1}{4L_{\Psi}}.

≤(ηt−1−ηt−1−1−2​c​ηt)​𝔼​[‖𝐳t‖2]+6​c2​ηt3​σ2+8​(1−βt)2​LΨ2ηt​𝔼​[‖𝐰t+1−𝐰t‖2]\displaystyle\leq(\eta_{t}^{-1}-\eta_{t-1}^{-1}-2c\eta_{t})\mathbb{E}[\|\mathbf{z}_{t}\|^{2}]+6c^{2}\eta_{t}^{3}\sigma^{2}+\frac{8(1-\beta_{t})^{2}L_{\Psi}^{2}}{\eta_{t}}\mathbb{E}[\|\mathbf{w}_{t+1}-\mathbf{w}_{t}\|^{2}] (31)

In the same way with Eq. (15) and ηt≤η1,∀t≥1\eta_{t}\leq\eta_{1},\forall t\geq 1, we could also have

By Theorem 1 in Arora et al. [2023], we have the following guarantee:

𝔼⁡[‖𝐯t+1−∇wg​(𝐰t+1)‖2]⩽τ2​η2​q​Ψ0T+η3​q​τ22​τ122​A+τ12\mathbb{E}[\|\mathbf{v}_{t+1}-\nabla_{w}g(\mathbf{w}_{t+1})\|^{2}]\leqslant\frac{\tau_{2}\eta^{2}q\Psi_{0}}{T}+\frac{\eta^{3}q\tau_{2}^{2}\tau_{1}^{2}}{2A}+\tau_{1}^{2}

where we define A=η2−L1​η22−η3​τ22​q2A=\frac{\eta}{2}-\frac{L_{1}\eta^{2}}{2}-\frac{\eta^{3}\tau_{2}^{2}q}{2}, τ12=O⁡(G2​T​Ad2q)\tau_{1}^{2}=O(\frac{G^{2}TA_{d}^{2}}{q}) and τ22=O⁡(L2b2+L2​T​Ad2)\tau_{2}^{2}=O(\frac{L^{2}}{b_{2}}+L^{2}TA_{d}^{2}), Ad=d​log⁡(1/δ)n​εA_{d}=\frac{\sqrt{d\log(1/\delta)}}{n\varepsilon}

By the same method as Theorem 2 in Xu et al. [2019], we have the following inequality,

‖𝐳t−∇Ψ​(𝐰t+1)+1ηt​(𝐰t−𝐰t+1)‖2⩽2​‖𝐳t−∇Ψ​(𝐰t)‖2+2​(Ψ⁡(𝐰t+1)−Ψ⁡(𝐰t))ηt+(2​LΨ2+3​LΨηt)​‖𝐰t+1−𝐰t‖2.\left\|\mathbf{z}_{t}-\nabla\Psi(\mathbf{w}_{t+1})+\frac{1}{\eta_{t}}(\mathbf{w}_{t}-\mathbf{w}_{t+1})\right\|^{2}\leqslant 2\left\|\mathbf{z}_{t}-\nabla\Psi(\mathbf{w}_{t})\right\|^{2}+\frac{2(\Psi(\mathbf{w}_{t+1})-\Psi(\mathbf{w}_{t}))}{\eta_{t}}+(2L_{\Psi}^{2}+\frac{3L_{\Psi}}{\eta_{t}})\left\|\mathbf{w}_{t+1}-\mathbf{w}_{t}\right\|^{2}.

Therefore, all we need to do is to bound the three terms. Actually, the first term can be bounded by Lemma 7 and then, then by the Lipschitz property of function Ψ⁡(𝐰)\Psi(\mathbf{w}), then it can be reduced to bound the term with ‖𝐰t+1−𝐰t‖2\left\|\mathbf{w}_{t+1}-\mathbf{w}_{t}\right\|^{2}

Since F⁡(𝐰)F(\mathbf{w}) is smooth with parameter LFL_{F}, then

Ψ⁡(𝐰t+1)≤Ψ⁡(𝐰t)+⟨∇Ψ​(𝐰t),𝐰t+1−𝐰t⟩+LΨ2​‖𝐰t+1−𝐰t‖2.\Psi(\mathbf{w}_{t+1})\leq\Psi(\mathbf{w}_{t})+\langle\nabla\Psi(\mathbf{w}_{t}),\mathbf{w}_{t+1}-\mathbf{w}_{t}\rangle+\frac{L_{\Psi}}{2}\|\mathbf{w}_{t+1}-\mathbf{w}_{t}\|^{2}. (39)

Combining the above two inequalities, we get

⟨𝐳t−∇F​(𝐰t),𝐰t+1−𝐰t⟩+12​(1/η−LΨ)​‖𝐰t+1−𝐰t‖2≤F⁡(𝐰t)−F⁡(𝐰t+1).\langle\mathbf{z}_{t}-\nabla F(\mathbf{w}_{t}),\mathbf{w}_{t+1}-\mathbf{w}_{t}\rangle+\frac{1}{2}(1/\eta-L_{\Psi})\|\mathbf{w}_{t+1}-\mathbf{w}_{t}\|^{2}\leq F(\mathbf{w}_{t})-F(\mathbf{w}_{t+1}). (40)

That is

12​(1/η−LΨ)​‖𝐰t+1−𝐰t‖2\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}(1/\eta-L_{\Psi})\|\mathbf{w}_{t+1}-\mathbf{w}_{t}\|^{2} ≤Ψ⁡(𝐰t)−Ψ⁡(𝐰t+1)−⟨𝐳t−∇ψ​(𝐰t),𝐰t+1−𝐰t⟩\displaystyle\leq\Psi(\mathbf{w}_{t})-\Psi(\mathbf{w}_{t+1})-\langle\mathbf{z}_{t}-\nabla\psi(\mathbf{w}_{t}),\mathbf{w}_{t+1}-\mathbf{w}_{t}\rangle (41)
≤Ψ⁡(𝐰t)−Ψ⁡(𝐰t+1)+η​‖𝐳t−∇Ψ​(𝐰t)‖2+14​η​‖𝐰t−𝐰t+1‖2,\displaystyle\leq\Psi(\mathbf{w}_{t})-\Psi(\mathbf{w}_{t+1})+\eta\|\mathbf{z}_{t}-\nabla\Psi(\mathbf{w}_{t})\|^{2}+\frac{1}{4\eta}\|\mathbf{w}_{t}-\mathbf{w}_{t+1}\|^{2}, (42)

where the last inequality uses Young’s inequality ⟨𝐚,𝐛⟩≤‖𝐚‖2+‖𝐛‖24\langle\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}\rangle\leq\|\mathbf{a}\|^{2}+\frac{\|\mathbf{b}\|^{2}}{4}. Then by rearranging the above inequality and summing it across t=1,⋯,Tt=1,\cdots,T, we have

∑t=1T1−2​η​LΨ4​η​‖𝐰t+1−𝐰t‖2\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{1-2\eta L_{\Psi}}{4\eta}\|\mathbf{w}_{t+1}-\mathbf{w}_{t}\|^{2} ≤Ψ⁡(𝐰1)−Ψ⁡(𝐰T+1)+∑t=1Tη​‖𝐳t−∇Ψ​(𝐰t)‖2\displaystyle\leq\Psi(\mathbf{w}_{1})-\Psi(\mathbf{w}_{T+1})+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta\|\mathbf{z}_{t}-\nabla\Psi(\mathbf{w}_{t})\|^{2}
≤Ψ⁡(𝐰1)−inf𝐰∈𝒲Ψ⁡(𝐰)+∑t=1Tη​‖𝐳t−∇Ψ​(𝐰t)‖2\displaystyle\leq\Psi(\mathbf{w}_{1})-\inf_{\mathbf{w}\in\mathcal{W}}\Psi(\mathbf{w})+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta\|\mathbf{z}_{t}-\nabla\Psi(\mathbf{w}_{t})\|^{2}
≤Ψ0+∑t=1Tη​‖𝐳t−∇Ψ​(𝐰t)‖2.\displaystyle\leq\Psi_{0}+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta\|\mathbf{z}_{t}-\nabla\Psi(\mathbf{w}_{t})\|^{2}. (43)

Thus,

1−2​η1​LΨ4​∑t=1T1ηt​‖𝐰t+1−𝐰t‖2≤∑t=1T1−2​ηt​LΨ4​ηt​‖𝐰t+1−𝐰t‖2≤Ψ0+∑t=1Tηt​‖𝐳t−∇Ψ​(𝐰t)‖2.\frac{1-2\eta_{1}L_{\Psi}}{4}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{1}{\eta_{t}}\|\mathbf{w}_{t+1}-\mathbf{w}_{t}\|^{2}\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{1-2\eta_{t}L_{\Psi}}{4\eta_{t}}\|\mathbf{w}_{t+1}-\mathbf{w}_{t}\|^{2}\leq\Psi_{0}+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}\|\mathbf{z}_{t}-\nabla\Psi(\mathbf{w}_{t})\|^{2}.

Dividing η11/4−η1​LΨ/2\frac{\eta_{1}}{1/4-\eta_{1}L_{\Psi}/2} on both sides for the above inequality, we have:

∑t=1T‖𝐰t+1−𝐰t‖2≤11/4−η1​LΨ/2​(η1​Ψ0+η1​∑t=1Tηt​‖𝐳t−∇Ψ​(𝐰t)‖2).\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|\mathbf{w}_{t+1}-\mathbf{w}_{t}\|^{2}\leq\frac{1}{1/4-\eta_{1}L_{\Psi}/2}\left(\eta_{1}\Psi_{0}+\eta_{1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\eta_{t}\|\mathbf{z}_{t}-\nabla\Psi(\mathbf{w}_{t})\|^{2}\right).

Therefore, combining the above inequality and choosing the parameter we set before, we can derive that

Appendix D Experimental Results

D.1 Test AUC Analysis

Figure 2 presents the Area Under the Curve (AUC) performance of four algorithms across different datasets. The AUC metric is particularly valuable as it measures the model’s ability to distinguish between classes regardless of the classification threshold, providing a comprehensive view of classifier performance.

Across the four datasets (CIFAR10-ST, CelebA, Fashion-MNIST, and MNIST-ST), we observe distinct performance patterns. The MNIST-ST dataset generally exhibits the highest AUC scores, which is expected given its relatively simple binary classification task with well-separated digit classes. Fashion-MNIST presents a more challenging scenario due to the visual similarity between certain clothing categories, resulting in comparatively lower AUC values. The CelebA dataset, dealing with facial attribute classification, demonstrates intermediate performance, while CIFAR10-ST shows varying convergence patterns depending on the algorithm employed.

The comparative analysis reveals that different algorithms exhibit varying degrees of robustness across datasets. Some algorithms demonstrate consistent performance across all datasets, suggesting good generalization capabilities, while others show dataset-specific strengths. The convergence behavior also varies, with some algorithms achieving stable AUC values earlier in training, while others require more iterations to reach optimal performance.

D.2 Test F1 Score Analysis

Figure 3 presents the F1 score results, which provide a harmonic mean of precision and recall. This metric is particularly important when dealing with imbalanced datasets or when both false positives and false negatives carry significant costs.

The F1 scores reveal nuanced performance differences that may not be immediately apparent from accuracy alone. For MNIST-ST, the F1 scores closely track accuracy values, confirming robust performance across both metrics. However, for potentially imbalanced scenarios in CelebA (where certain facial attributes may be rare), the F1 score provides critical insights into the model’s ability to correctly identify minority class instances without sacrificing precision.

On Fashion-MNIST F1 scores indicate how well algorithms balance precision and recall when distinguishing between similar clothing categories. Lower F1 scores compared to accuracy might suggest that while overall accuracy is reasonable, the model struggles with specific class pairs, leading to either high false positive or false negative rates for certain categories.

CIFAR10-ST F1 scores demonstrate the algorithms’ effectiveness in handling the complexity of natural images. The relationship between F1 scores and accuracy across different algorithms reveals which approaches better balance the trade-off between precision and recall. Algorithms showing F1 scores close to their accuracy values indicate balanced performance, while larger gaps suggest potential issues with either over-prediction or under-prediction of certain classes.

Overall, the F1 score analysis complements the AUC and accuracy metrics by highlighting the algorithms’ ability to maintain balanced performance across different evaluation criteria, which is essential for practical deployment scenarios.
